what_its_for: Oxcarbazepine is used to treat seizures (epilepsy). It works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain that cause seizures. It may be used alone or along with other seizure medicines.
how_to_take: Take oxcarbazepine by mouth exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Swallow extended-release tablets (Oxtellar XR) whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. If you are taking the liquid form, shake the bottle well before each use and use the measuring syringe provided, not a kitchen spoon. Try to take it at the same time(s) each day to keep the medicine working steadily in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your age, weight, and how well your kidneys work. Most adults start at a low dose and gradually increase over a few weeks. Do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine on your own — stopping suddenly can cause serious seizures. Always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store oxcarbazepine tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid bottle tightly closed and use it within 7 weeks of opening. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking oxcarbazepine — it can increase dizziness and drowsiness and may worsen side effects. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Be careful in hot weather or when exercising, as oxcarbazepine can cause low sodium levels (hyponatremia) which may be worsened by excessive sweating. Talk to your doctor before taking hormonal birth control (pills, patches, rings) — oxcarbazepine can make them less effective, so use a backup method of contraception.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of harming yourself or suicide, a new or worsening skin rash (especially with blisters or peeling), swelling of your face, lips, or throat, trouble breathing, signs of low sodium such as nausea, headache, confusion, extreme tiredness, or seizures that are worse or more frequent, vision changes or double vision, or signs of an allergic reaction. Also tell your doctor if you become pregnant or are planning to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Oxcarbazepine starts working within a few days of starting treatment, but it may take several weeks of dose adjustments before your seizures are fully controlled. Do not stop taking it even if you feel fine — seizure medicine must be taken consistently to keep working. Your doctor will monitor your progress with follow-up visits and possibly blood tests.
special_populations: Children: Oxcarbazepine is approved for children as young as 2 years old for certain uses. The dose is based on the child's weight and will be adjusted as they grow. Older adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and low sodium. Regular blood tests to check sodium levels are important. Kidney problems: If your kidneys do not work well, your doctor may start you at a lower dose and monitor you more closely. Pregnancy: Oxcarbazepine may harm an unborn baby. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits. Do not stop the medicine on your own. Breastfeeding: Oxcarbazepine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding.
